terms.definition: The technical field of designing, building, evaluating, and operating useful applications and systems by using pretrained foundation models (mainly LLMs) as components. The focus is less on creating a model from scratch and more on selecting models, connecting them to data and tools, and running an evaluation-and-improvement cycle.

A development approach that repeats build → measure → fix. Because AI application outputs vary probabilistically, quality is judged using evaluation data and metrics rather than intuition; the results are used to improve prompts, data, models, and tools. In this course, we use a learning-support agent as the topic and continue this cycle across multiple lectures.

A model trained on a large amount of text that predicts the next token given the input and generates text. It can handle many tasks, such as question answering, summarization, and code generation, simply by changing the instructions (prompt).

The smallest unit of text handled by an LLM. It is split into fragments of words or characters. API costs, rate limits, and context window size are often counted in tokens. Japanese text tends to use more tokens per character than English.

The maximum total number of input and output tokens that an LLM can handle in a single call. Since conversation history and tool results also need to fit within this limit, designing what to pass to the model is crucial.
The input text passed to an LLM. It can contain not only the question but also the role, constraints, output format, examples, and more to guide the model output.
Input provided separately from the user question to specify the model behavior (role, tone, rules to follow, etc.). In Pydantic AI, this is passed via the Agent instructions argument.

A setting that controls the randomness when choosing the next token. Lower values make outputs more stable, while higher values make them more diverse. It is one reason the same question can produce different answers.

A phenomenon in which an LLM generates content that contradicts facts or invents information in a convincing way. It is more likely to occur when the model is asked about things it does not know, such as up-to-date information or course-specific details. It can be reduced by having the model reference external data through tools, provide evidence, and detect it through evaluation.
A gateway for programs to call functions exposed by another service. In this course, we use the Gemini API from Python to use the LLM.

A secret string used to identify who is calling the API. If it leaks, others can consume your quota. Do not write it directly in code, do not commit it, and do not paste it into chat. In this course, we register it as a Codespaces secret and load it as the environment variable GEMINI_API_KEY.
A value set outside the program (in the OS or runtime environment) and read by the program by name. It is used to keep secrets such as API keys and environment-specific settings separate from code.

The maximum number of requests or tokens allowed within a given time period. Exceeding it returns errors such as HTTP 429. Free tiers are especially strict, and agents often hit the limit because they call the LLM multiple times for one question.

A cloud-based development environment provided by GitHub. You can open VS Code in the browser and immediately use an environment configured according to the repository settings. Personal accounts have a free monthly quota, and if you do not stop the environment, usage continues to be consumed.

A mechanism for defining a development environment as a container. By writing the Python version, extensions, and startup commands in .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, the same environment is available regardless of who opens Codespaces.

A secret value registered in GitHub account settings. It is passed to the environment when a specified repository's Codespaces is started. You must choose the repository to use when registering it (your own fork). If you register it while a Codespace is running, you need to restart the Codespace.
A complete copy of someone else's repository under your own account. In this course, we fork the course repository and do our work and submissions on our own fork.
A mechanism for separating work streams. You can try changes without breaking main and then merge them via PR. In this course, we create work branches such as lec01 for each lecture.

A mechanism for requesting that changes from one branch be merged into another. It supports diff review, comments, and display of automated test results. In this course, submissions are made as PRs from a work branch in your fork to main.
GitHub's AI coding assistant. It supports code completion in the editor, chat-based Q&A, and multi-file editing in agent mode. Copilot Free has limits on the number of completions and chat usage.

A feature in which AI suggests the rest of code based on partially written code or comments. It is accepted with Tab. Suggestions are not always correct, so read and understand them before adopting them.

An AI system that uses files and command execution as tools and autonomously works through programming tasks over multiple steps. Examples include Claude Code, Copilot agent mode, and Pi. The underlying structure is the same as AI agents in general: LLM + loop + tools.
The initial stage in which a model is trained on large amounts of general text to predict the next token. Much of a language model's general knowledge and common sense is acquired here.

The process of further training a pretrained model on task-specific or format-specific data. It is useful for adapting output format, tone, or behavior for a particular domain. For learning the latest facts, it is often better to make the model reference external data via tools or RAG than to rely on fine-tuning alone.
A method of additional training that uses pairs of input and desired output (e.g., questions and examples of ideal answers). It is a representative method for teaching a model to follow instructions.

A general term for methods that train only a small subset of the model's parameters or a small set of added parameters, rather than all model parameters. This substantially reduces required GPU memory and storage. LoRA is the representative example.

A PEFT method that keeps the pretrained weights fixed while representing the update as the product of two small matrices (a low-rank matrix). Only these small matrices are trained. Since the trainable parameters are small, the saved adapter file is also small. We use LoRA in lecture 2's exercises.
A hyperparameter that determines the size of the low-rank matrix used in LoRA. Larger values increase expressive power but also increase trainable parameters and memory usage.

A method that quantizes the base model weights to 4 bits or similar to save memory, then performs training with LoRA. This allows larger models to run on smaller GPUs. In this course's lecture 2 exercises, we train a model with LoRA and compare memory usage and output differences when loaded in 4-bit mode in the extension tasks.
A technique that represents model weights with fewer bits (e.g., 16-bit to 4-bit) to reduce memory usage and computation. Accuracy may decrease slightly.
A hyperparameter that determines how far parameters move in one update. If it is too high, training becomes unstable; if too low, progress is slow.
A full pass through the entire training dataset counts as one epoch. If the number is increased too much, overfitting becomes more likely.
A state in which the model fits the training data too closely and performance drops on unseen inputs. It is noticed by measuring performance on validation data that is not used for training.
A platform for sharing and downloading public models and datasets. It is used to obtain open-weight models and publish LoRA adapters.
A system in which an LLM decides for itself which tools to call, sees the results, and decides the next action in a loop to achieve a goal. The basic structure is model + loop + tools.

A process where input is passed to the model, the model returns a tool call, the tool is executed, and the result is returned to the model, repeating until the model returns a final answer. Since one question can trigger multiple LLM calls, the impact on time, cost, and rate limits is significant.

A function prepared so that the model can call it. The model sees the tool name, description, and argument types, decides when to call it and with which arguments, and the program executes it. It is used for searches, calculations, file operations, and external API calls.

The text that explains the purpose of the tool and the meaning of its arguments to the model. In Pydantic AI, it is automatically generated from the function's docstring and type hints. Because the model reads this to decide whether to use the tool and which arguments to pass, the wording can significantly change behavior.
A mechanism for receiving the model's output in a predetermined format or JSON schema. This makes downstream processing in code easier. In Pydantic AI, you specify a Pydantic model with output_type.

A program that wraps around the LLM with a loop, tools, and interface (UI) so it can perform actual work. Claude Code and Pi are examples of a harness. Pi is known as a thin harness that narrows its built-in tools to read, write, edit, and bash.

An open-source coding agent that runs in the terminal (MIT license). It is composed of minimal functionality and a system prompt, and is designed so users can extend it. Version 1.0 was released in October 2026. The npm package name is @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent.

A framework for building agents in Python. It allows you to define tool arguments and outputs using Pydantic types, and it supports many models such as Gemini and OpenAI with the same code style. It can also be tested without calling the real API using a test model. This is the main line of lecture 3.

An open-source agent development framework published by Google. It is deeply integrated with Gemini, and adk web lets you visually inspect the flow of tool calls. Version 2.0 introduced breaking changes from 1.x. We cover it at the advanced homework level in this course.

An open standard protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools and data sources. Tools published as MCP servers can be used by various compatible agents and editors (MCP clients) through the same method. In lecture 5, we experience putting glossary search behind an MCP server.

Constraints or checks designed to prevent an agent from taking undesirable actions or producing poor output. Methods include rules in the prompt, limiting tool permissions, checking the output, and requiring human approval before critical actions.

Embedding human confirmation or approval in the middle of an agent's process. This is used before irreversible operations such as writing data or sending messages. In Pydantic AI, it can be implemented with tools that set requires_approval=True.

A fake test model included in Pydantic AI. Instead of calling a real LLM, it triggers tool calls and returns dummy responses. This lets you test agent wiring—whether the tool is registered, called, and the result is returned—without using API keys or quota.

The structure of homework in AIE2026: “Basic” (checking lecture content), “Implementation” (writing code yourself), and “Advanced” (research and experimentation). Completing any one level completes the homework for that lecture. Grading is generally not done.

The file in which results for each lecture's exercise or homework are written in AIE2026. It is located at lectures/NN/answer.md. Fill in the level attempted, what you did, the results, and insights, then submit it by creating a PR from your work branch to main in your fork.

A Git tag in the AIE2026 course repo used to mark the starting code for each lecture exercise (for example: lec03-start). Even if a previous lecture is not complete, you can create a branch from this tag to begin that lecture's exercise.

The standard model used for AIE2026 exercises and homework is gemini-3.5-flash-lite. It was chosen to balance free-tier rate limits and the stability of course operations. You may switch to another model using the AIE_MODEL environment variable, or use your own paid API if you have one.

Using functionality outside the agent's program as a tool, such as fetching web pages, file operations, databases, or third-party APIs. The function tools from lecture 3 run inside the same process, while external tools are called across process or machine boundaries. MCP provides a common convention for this.

The program that exposes tools (and resources, prompts) through MCP. What is published is the tool name, description, and argument schema; the client requests the tool, the server executes it, and returns the result. In this course, we turn glossary search into an MCP server (app/mcp_server.py). Many packaged servers are also available (fetch, filesystem, GitHub, etc.).

The side that connects to an MCP server, passes the published tools to the model, and calls tools according to the model's instructions. An agent program (such as Pydantic AI's MCPToolset) or editors/apps such as Copilot Chat, Claude Desktop, and Cursor can act as clients. The advantage of MCP is that the same server can be used from any client.

The communication path between the MCP client and server. In stdio mode, the client starts the server as a subprocess and exchanges messages over standard input/output (simple and convenient for use on the same machine). In Streamable HTTP mode, the server listens at a URL and can be accessed from other processes or machines (requiring attention to exposure and authentication).

A configuration file listing the MCP servers to use. For each server, write its name and startup command (stdio) or connection URL (HTTP). Claude Desktop, Cursor, and Pydantic AI read the same mcpServers format (VS Code / Copilot Chat uses the servers format instead). In this course, the file is app/mcp_servers.json. The core MCP experience is that adding a few lines of configuration increases the available tools.

When multiple MCP servers are used, the same tool names are distinguished by prefixing them with the server name as server_name_tool_name. In this course, app/agent.py automatically adds the server name from the config file (e.g., glossary_search_glossary). Pydantic AI's load_mcp_toolsets does the same. As the number of tools increases, the descriptions passed to the model also increase, which affects both tool selection accuracy and token usage.

A prebuilt MCP server that retrieves the specified URL page and returns the body as Markdown (Python-based, started with uvx mcp-server-fetch). In this course, it is used as an example of “adding external tools just by writing in the config file.” Because the model accesses the URL it selects, the user must be aware of where data is being sent.
